Family Health

Hawthorn while breastfeeding: fruit, supplements and uncertain safety

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hawthorn fruit and hawthorn herbal products are not interchangeable. There is no reliable evidence that hawthorn improves milk supply or milk quality, and its safety for a breastfed baby has not been established. Before using it as a remedy, review the actual product with a pharmacist or clinician and seek feeding support if supply is a concern.

What is hawthorn?

Hawthorn refers to Crataegus plants in the rose family, also known by names such as may tree or shan zha. These often thorny, deciduous shrubs or small trees have spring flower clusters and small apple-like fruits that ripen later in the year. Leaves, fruit colours, height and the number of hard stones vary by species; common hawthorn has lobed leaves, pale flowers and red fruit with one stone.

Hedgerow use and a long food history do not make every wild berry edible or identify a product. Do not rely on a photograph or common name for foraging, and do not eat the hard seeds. Fruit eaten as food is a different exposure from concentrated leaf, flower, fruit or root preparations; a botanical description cannot establish breastfeeding safety.

Antioxidants and traditional claims are not clinical proof

Hawthorn contains flavonoids and other polyphenols. Antioxidant activity in a laboratory does not prove treatment benefits. Traditional claims include improved mood or depression, relief of grief, cognition, eyesight, seizures, headaches, energy, fatigue, detox, metabolism and fat burning. These are not established breastfeeding treatments, and there is no evidence that hawthorn causes weight loss.

Other claims concern hair growth, bones, blood sugar, blood fats, bile and digestion of heavy meals, intestinal infections, worms or dysentery, tuberculosis, skin aging or eczema, and kidney stones. Do not substitute hawthorn for assessment or effective treatment of these conditions. A plant compound or traditional use is not proof of a safe medicine.

Heart claims need particular caution

Hawthorn is promoted as a heart tonic for rhythm, contraction strength, circulation, stress tolerance, clot prevention and chronic heart failure. Human heart-failure studies have conflicting results, and evidence is insufficient for many other heart claims. Possible effects on vessels or heart cells do not establish that a fruit or supplement prevents clots or treats an arrhythmia.

Some European leaf-and-flower products have traditional-use recognition for mild nervous cardiac complaints after serious illness has been excluded, or mild stress and sleep symptoms. This is not approval as a breastfeeding remedy. The final EMA monograph is from 2016; the 2025 revision is a draft. Do not replace prescribed cardiac treatment or self-treat chest symptoms.

Does hawthorn increase milk or improve its quality?

No valid clinical trial establishes hawthorn as a milk booster. LactMed describes an old, very small study reporting changes in milk volume and fat, but it lacked adequate controls and blinding. It cannot establish a dependable benefit, a dose, or better infant nourishment. Traditional claims about richer or more plentiful milk are not sufficient evidence.

There are no useful published measurements of hawthorn components in human milk or breastfed infants, and infant safety data are lacking. A rise in a hormone or laboratory antioxidant finding would not by itself prove improved milk transfer or infant growth. Do not give hawthorn tea, drops or supplements directly to a baby.

Is the fruit safer than a supplement?

Ordinary fruit, strong tea, tinctures, capsules and extracts differ in plant part, concentration and other ingredients. Studies of one standardized extract cannot establish the safety of another product. Food use also does not supply a proven breastfeeding-safe amount; avoid interpreting “in moderation” as a validated dose.

The NHS advises against herbal medicines during breastfeeding because there is not enough evidence to guarantee safety. The EMA leaf-and-flower monograph also does not recommend use during lactation because data are insufficient. If you want to eat hawthorn fruit or have already used a product, discuss the actual exposure individually rather than assuming either certain harm or certain safety.

Possible side effects and medicine interactions

Adult reports include dizziness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and other abdominal discomfort; headache, fatigue or rash may occur. Confusion, sleep changes, nosebleeds, marked low blood pressure, palpitations and an irregular heartbeat are sometimes attributed to hawthorn, but these are not all predictable effects of ordinary fruit. Toxicity or overdose can involve low blood pressure and rhythm problems; breastfeeding-specific rates are unknown.

Ask a pharmacist to check heart medicines, digoxin, blood-pressure treatment, blood thinners and diabetes medicines alongside every supplement. Some proposed interactions come from laboratory findings and their clinical importance is uncertain; not every combination is proven harmful. Mention upcoming surgery and unusual bleeding. Do not stop necessary prescribed medicines or change doses yourself to accommodate hawthorn.

Product quality: a specific root-supplement warning

In its September 2026 update, the FDA warned that certain products sold for weight loss, including some labelled tejocote or Mexican hawthorn root, contained toxic yellow oleander. This can cause serious gastrointestinal, neurological and heart problems, including death. The warning concerns particular adulterated products, not evidence that all ordinary hawthorn fruit contains oleander.

Check the actual product against official safety alerts. Do not use a product named in the warning; if you took one, stop using it and contact a clinician immediately, even if use was not recent. Severe symptoms need emergency care. Keep the packaging; a label, “natural” claim or online sale cannot guarantee identity or quality.

If you have already consumed hawthorn

Record whether it was fruit, tea, extract or a mixed product, the amount and dates, ingredients, medicines and any symptoms. Give the clinician your baby’s age, prematurity or jaundice history and feeding pattern. Pause further unsupervised medicinal use while obtaining advice; one exposure alone does not prove that your baby has been harmed.

There is no evidence-based universal waiting period, milk-discard schedule or automatic reason to wean after hawthorn. A clinician can assess the product and whether any temporary feeding plan is needed. Do not induce vomiting, try a home detox or stop necessary prescribed treatment. Suspected poisoning or known harmful ingestion needs immediate emergency care; if you are unsure whether a product is harmful, obtain urgent poison-service or medical advice. If poisoning is suspected, do not eat or drink anything while waiting for medical help. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

Low supply concerns need a feeding assessment

Ask a trained breastfeeding professional to observe a feed and assess latch, swallowing, effective milk removal, age-appropriate wet nappies and weight gain. Maternal or infant illness, medicines and feeding difficulties may need treatment. A balanced varied diet supports health, but no special fruit is required to make good-quality milk.

Agree a practical feeding or expressing plan and follow-up for both you and your baby. If additional milk is needed, use an individualized supplementation plan rather than delaying it for a herbal trial. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment; do not wait for a supplement to work.

Symptoms that must not wait

Seek emergency care for persistent palpitations that do not settle, or palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or feeling faint; fainting or loss of consciousness and severe breathing difficulty also need emergency help. If concerning palpitations have stopped, arrange urgent medical assessment. Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, or faintness after a possible allergic reaction needs emergency help; a rash is not required. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

For a baby, breathing difficulty, blue, grey or unusually pale skin, a seizure, being difficult to wake or unresponsive, or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. Poor feeding or dehydration signs need urgent assessment even without all these signs. Do not assume a symptom is caused by hawthorn or delay help while checking an app or product label. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Avoid using hawthorn as a milk booster. Ask a trained feeding professional to assess milk transfer, infant growth and any underlying cause; agree supplementation and follow-up when needed.

Show a pharmacist or clinician the actual fruit or herbal product, label, amounts, dates and medicine list, including your baby’s age and health. Ask about individual exposure rather than assuming a safe dose or automatically discarding milk.

Check product safety alerts, avoid named adulterated products and seek immediate advice after their use. Use urgent or emergency care for warning symptoms without delaying for tracking or supplement research.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record feeds, wet nappies, product labels, medicines, symptoms and questions for appointments. It cannot diagnose low supply, establish herbal safety or assess poisoning; feeding difficulties and warning symptoms need professional care.

When to seek help

Avoid unsupervised medicinal hawthorn while breastfeeding; no safe dose or milk-boosting benefit is established. Poor infant feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment. Breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale skin, seizures, difficulty waking or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. Severe allergic symptoms, persistent palpitations or palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness, and fainting or loss of consciousness need emergency care. Do not stop necessary prescribed medicines yourself; suspected poisoning or known harmful ingestion needs immediate emergency care. If you are unsure whether a product is harmful, obtain urgent medical or poison-service advice. If poisoning is suspected, do not eat or drink anything while waiting for medical help. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Hawthorn has no reliable milk-supply or milk-quality benefit, and infant safety has not been established.
  • Fruit and concentrated herbal preparations differ; no breastfeeding-safe hawthorn dose is proven.
  • Review the actual product and medicines with a clinician or pharmacist; do not stop necessary prescribed treatment yourself.
  • Feeding concerns and warning symptoms need assessed care, not a herbal trial.

Frequently asked questions

Are the traditional benefits proven?

Claims about mood, heart health, digestion, infections, skin, metabolism and other conditions are not all established. Heart-failure studies are mixed and laboratory antioxidant activity does not prove clinical benefit. Do not use hawthorn instead of effective treatment.

Does hawthorn increase milk supply or improve milk quality?

No valid trial establishes either benefit. A very small old uncontrolled study cannot show that hawthorn reliably increases milk, improves infant nourishment or supplies a useful dose. Feeding assessment is the first step for a supply concern.

Is eating hawthorn while breastfeeding safe?

Safety for a breastfed baby is not established. Ordinary fruit differs from medicinal extracts, but “moderation” is not a proven safe dose. Ask about the actual product and exposure; NHS advice recommends avoiding herbal medicines during breastfeeding.

What side effects are possible?

Adult reports include dizziness and digestive symptoms; toxicity can involve low blood pressure or an irregular heartbeat. Many other attributed symptoms and breastfeeding-specific risks remain uncertain. New symptoms need assessment, and severe reactions need emergency care.

Should I stop breastfeeding after one exposure?

One exposure does not prove harm or automatically require weaning. Keep the label and discuss the amount, preparation, timing, baby’s age and health, and medicines with a clinician. There is no universal milk-discard or waiting schedule; any temporary feeding plan must be individualized.

Can hawthorn interact with medicines?

Possible interactions concern cardiac medicines, digoxin, blood-pressure treatment, blood thinners and diabetes medicines, but some evidence is theoretical or limited. A pharmacist should review your full list and surgery plans. Do not change necessary prescribed treatment yourself.

What if I used a tejocote-root weight-loss product?

Check current FDA alerts for the exact product. Certain products contained toxic yellow oleander. Stop a named product and contact a clinician immediately even if use was not recent; severe symptoms need emergency care. This warning does not mean all hawthorn fruit is adulterated.

When do feeding or reaction symptoms need help?

Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or unusual drowsiness needs prompt assessment. A baby with breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale skin, a seizure, difficulty waking or no urine for 12 hours needs immediate emergency care. Severe allergy signs, persistent palpitations or palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness, and fainting or loss of consciousness need emergency care; do not wait for every sign. For emergency care, do not drive yourself; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
